Text: The system of units most important in physics today is abbreviated SI, which stands for {{c1::Système International}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: Système International is French for "International System."

Distinguish: SI is not the only system of units in use — the cgs system and the British engineering system are two others.

Text: The system of units now known as the SI used to be called the {{c1::MKS::acronym}} system.
Back Extra:
Meaning: MKS stands for meter-kilogram-second — the three standards the system is built on.

Distinguish: MKS and cgs are both metric systems, but MKS builds on the meter and kilogram while cgs builds on the centimeter and gram.

Text: The British engineering system's standards are the foot for length, the second for time, and the pound for {{c1::force::force or mass}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the metric systems standardize mass in that slot — the kilogram in SI, the gram in cgs — while the British engineering system standardizes a force.

Cue: the British engineering system is used more in the U.S. than in Britain.

Text: The SI is built on {{c1::seven::number of base quantities}} base quantities — the smallest number consistent with a full description of the physical world.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the SI is not just the meter, second, and kilogram — four more base quantities sit alongside those three.

Roster: length, time, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.

Text:
Apart from length, time, and mass, the SI's other four base quantities are:

{{c1::electric current}}

{{c1::temperature}}

{{c1::amount of substance}}

{{c1::luminous intensity}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: length, time, and mass are the mechanical three; the other four are what a mechanics-only description of nature leaves out.

Roster: length, time, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.

Text: In the SI, the base quantity {{c1::electric current}} is measured in {{c2::amperes (A)}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: electric current is the one electrical base quantity — charge, voltage, and resistance are not among the SI's base quantities.

Roster: length, time, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.

Text: In the SI, the base quantity {{c1::temperature}} is measured in {{c2::kelvins (K)}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the degree Celsius is not an SI base unit — only the kelvin is, and its abbreviation carries no degree sign.

Roster: length, time, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.

Text: In the SI, the base quantity {{c1::amount of substance}} is measured in {{c2::moles (mol)}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: amount of substance and mass are two separate SI base quantities — the mole does not measure how heavy something is.

Roster: length, time, mass, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity.
